g.passage: Who brings a ferry token to a wedding? Mele wondered, watching Leilani turn the brass coin across her knuckles while the band tuned up in the crowded Auckland hall. Years ago, on stormy mornings, Leilani's father had pressed one into each passenger's hand at the gangway and collected it again on the far shore; a token, he liked to say, was only ever surrendered by someone who had arrived. Tonight Mele was waiting on a message from the hospital, where her brother had been in surgery since noon. During the speeches, Leilani set the coin in Mele's palm without a word. Mele held it through the toasts and the first dance, rubbing its worn rim whenever her phone stayed dark. When the screen finally lit, she did not read it at once; she closed her fingers around the brass first, then looked. Across the room, guests clapped as the couple cut a cake iced with tiny white sails.
g.question: In the text, the ferry token most likely represents
options: the fare that Mele still owes for the many crossings she once made on the ferry.
Leilani's longing for the harbor life she left behind when her father retired.
the newly married couple's hope for a long and steady voyage through marriage.
an assurance of safe passage that Mele holds onto as she waits for word.

g.passage: Cut grass and wet chalk are what I remember of the Taipei field the week after I missed the penalty in front of the whole stadium. Coach Yuxuan benched me without a word of explanation. Each evening at dusk she handed me a flat ball from the shed and a hand pump, and I knelt by the sideline while the others ran drills. I pumped carelessly at first, and by morning the ball sagged again, soft as my own legs had felt at the spot. Midweek I began to check the valve, press the seams, and test the bounce against my palm before returning it. Yuxuan said nothing about this; she only began handing me the ball a little earlier each night. On the seventh evening she bounced it once, hard, on the grass and nodded toward the goal. Overhead, the floodlights buzzed awake one bank at a time, and moths gathered in the glare.

options: the routine chores that Yuxuan assigns to teach Ruoxi obedience to team rules.

g.passage: Jeju Island had only one bus stop on that stretch of the mountain road, a tin shelter where Minjun waited after school. On Monday she had told a single classmate, in a whisper behind the gym, that her father was not coming back from Busan. By Wednesday the fishmonger had stopped charging her for squid, and the nurse at the clinic had squeezed her shoulder for no reason she could name. On Friday Eamon, who had fished beside her father for twenty years, sat down in the shelter and said her aunt had heard. The news had grown legs of its own, he added, and had not asked her permission to use them. He offered her a tangerine and said her aunt was not angry, only sorry to have learned it from a neighbor. Minjun peeled the fruit slowly. Mist slid over the ridge, and the bus appeared, its headlights soft in the gray.
g.question: As used in the text, the phrase “grown legs of its own” most nearly suggests that the news
options: had been exaggerated by each neighbor until it no longer matched the truth.
had traveled slowly because few people in the village cared to repeat it.
had moved from one person to another in ways Minjun could not direct.
had been carried by Eamon himself on his walk down to her aunt's house.
g.explanation: Minjun은 월요일에 친구 한 명에게만 이야기했지만, 수요일에는 생선 장수와 간호사가, 금요일에는 고모까지 그 사실을 알게 된다. 또 Eamon은 소식이 그녀의 허락을 구하지 않았다고 덧붙인다. 이 단서들을 이으면 '스스로 다리가 생겼다'는 표현은 소식이 Minjun의 통제를 벗어나 사람들 사이로 퍼졌다는 뜻이므로 C가 정답이다. A는 내용이 왜곡되었다는 근거가 없고, B는 사흘 만에 퍼진 속도와 맞지 않으며, D는 '걸어 내려간다'는 비유를 Eamon의 실제 행동으로 오해한 것이다.

seed.conflict: over a recipe that was never written down

g.passage: Kyoto's eastern hills were slick with rain when the funicular stalled halfway up, and the attendant led its two passengers onto a terrace café to wait. Takeshi took the table farthest from Kenji, nodded once, and opened a newspaper he did not read. Kenji ordered tea and remarked on the weather to no one in particular. For twenty minutes their only exchange concerned the sugar bowl. Then the owner set down a dish of pickled plums, and Kenji, tasting one, said quietly that his late grandmother had made them saltier, with a shiso leaf folded inside each. Takeshi lowered the paper. His mother had done the same, he said, and had never written the method down. Kenji pulled his chair across the terrace. Soon a napkin between them was crowded with figures, half of them crossed out, and each man was insisting, between bursts of laughter, that the leaves must dry a day longer or a day less. Below the railing, rain kept dripping from the maples into the moss.
g.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the text?
options: From reserved distance to lively, shared enthusiasm

From mild irritation to grudging, polite acceptance

g.passage: I sold the lamp. That was how I, Astrid, began my confession to Nargis when she found me at the open-air market in Tromso one Saturday in 1911. She had come north to survey the coast and had lodged two months at my lighthouse. On her first night she admired my father's brass lamp, calling it the only warm thing in the tower. Each dawn after that, I watched her leave for the fjord in a coat cut for a southern autumn, and each evening she stamped her feet a long while by the stove. Once she joked that her boots let in more sea than they kept out. While she was measuring inlets, I carried the lamp down the hill. With the coins I bought heavy wool and paid the cobbler's stall to resole her boots. Around us fish sellers shouted prices, and gulls quarreled over a dropped herring.
g.question: Based on the text, why does the narrator most likely sell the lamp?
options: She feels guilty that her father's lamp has gone unused since his death.

g.passage: Cairo had stayed behind on the far side of the canal, and the farmhouse I had rented seemed to belong to no city at all. On my first morning, Thida showed me the lemon tree by the well, a graft she had bound to a wild root years before. A pale ring still marked where the two barks had met and, for a season, refused to agree. When she asked how long I meant to stay, I said I had not unpacked enough to know. Thida only tightened the old twine around a new cutting and said grafts take best when no one hovers over them. I hovered anyway. Each evening before supper I walked to the tree and pressed my thumb to the ring, as if checking a pulse, and afterward I unpacked one more box. By the month's end a single green shoot had pushed out just above the scar. In the kitchen the kettle whistled, and the shutters knocked against the frame in the wind.
g.question: In the text, the grafted lemon tree most likely symbolizes
options: Thida's long devotion to the farmhouse garden and its earlier tenants

g.passage: Ramses Station, in the autumn of 1987, kept a narrow cafe beside platform four where students waited out delays over sweet tea. Every Thursday Yasmin came there to pay Karim, her younger brother's tutor, from an envelope she had counted twice at home. He always handed back the last coin, claiming with a grin that inflation had not yet reached algebra. Yasmin did not argue. On her way out, she dropped the coin into a chipped glass jar by the register, where the waiter gathered change for the boy who swept the platforms. Some weeks later Karim, finishing his tea, began dropping his own spare piastres in after hers. By spring the jar was nearly full, its coins dulled from handling, and the sweeping boy wore a pair of new shoes. When the trains at last ran on time again, the cafe rearranged its tables, and the jar moved to a shelf above the sugar.

g.passage: Sunethra kept the keeper's lodge at the reservoir above Lisbon in the drought year of 1868, and I was the hiker who stumbled out of her pines after two nights astray. She fed me, dried my boots by her stove, and asked little except whether anyone was waiting for me in the city. On the third morning she walked me to the end of the dock, where a lantern hung on a post, and lit it although the sun was already high. A handshake would do, I told her, laughing. She said her lantern did not care what I thought it should do. From the ridge, an hour later, I looked back and found the small flame still burning above the water, long after the lodge had vanished behind the trees. I walked the rest of the way more slowly than I needed to. Years afterward, when I told the story, I could never recall whether I had waved.

g.passage: When Camila found the photograph in my old sea chest, she carried it out to the orchard where I sat among the dead mango trees. In the picture I was twenty, grinning on a freighter's deck, my arm around a man I had not mentioned in forty years. Dario, she asked, who is he? I told her the trees had stopped bearing the summer I came home. She did not let me change the subject; she set the photograph on my knee and waited. The memory lay in my chest like an anchor fouled on the seabed, and every attempt I made to raise it only drew the line tight. Then, with her still beside me, saying nothing, I began to tell her about the storm off Veracruz. Camila listened, peeling a dry branch into strips, while the wind moved through the bare limbs overhead.
g.question: As used in the text, the phrase “like an anchor fouled on the seabed” most nearly suggests that the memory
options: had kept the narrator steady through his many lonely years ashore.

g.passage:
When the mourners left the hall in Chengdu,
Jianguo and I walked to the salt-water baths
our grandfather had built in the year of floods.
Eleni, he asked, you passed your examinations?
I nodded, and the lie went under
like a stone into the brine,
where nothing sinks quite all the way.

We sat on the tiled edge, feet in the green water.
He spoke of the ledger he had kept for the old man,
of figures he had copied twice.
All the while I kept glancing down,
as if something pale might rise

Above the pool the paper lanterns swung,

g.passage: What does a town do when its two oldest customs both claim the same evening? In the Riga suburb where I grew up, the answer was worked out in 1991 at the back of Vesna's shoe repair stall, because she was mayor and the stall had the only table long enough. Pavel, the town's only doctor, wanted the midsummer supper to follow his family's Orthodox fast; Vesna's neighbors wanted the old Latvian songs and the cheese with caraway. For an hour they argued over awls and heel nails. Then Pavel picked up a needle from the bench and said the whole matter was a question of stitching. Two leathers of different grain, he explained, could still be sewn into a single sole if the thread was patient. By midnight the menu listed the fasting dishes and the caraway cheese on facing halves of one card. Vesna's stall sells phones now, though the long table still stands in the back.
g.question: As used in the text, the phrase “sewn into a single sole” most nearly suggests
options: patching over an argument so that no one would raise it again
uniting two distinct customs in a single shared supper
replacing both old customs with a new tradition of the town's own
settling the dispute by letting one custom absorb the other
